title: Physics: Formulas and Constants

sources.name: 2022 CODATA recommended constants, published reference table
sources.license: Reference only; numerical facts, original wording

description: For intermediate physics students reviewing mechanics, fluids, heat, waves, optics, circuits, fields, and modern physics. Formulas define variables and state important idealizations; constants use SI units.

cards.front: What is Average velocity in one dimension?
cards.back: v_avg = displacement / elapsed time = (x_f - x_i)/Delta t. It includes direction through the sign.

cards.front: What is Average speed?
cards.back: Average speed = total distance traveled / elapsed time. It need not equal the magnitude of average velocity.

cards.front: What is Average acceleration?
cards.back: a_avg = (v_f - v_i)/Delta t, using signed velocities in one dimension or vectors in multiple dimensions.

cards.front: What is Instantaneous velocity?
cards.back: v = dx/dt in one dimension; vector velocity is the time derivative of position.

cards.front: What is Instantaneous acceleration?
cards.back: a = dv/dt = d^2x/dt^2 in one dimension.

cards.front: What is Velocity under constant acceleration?
cards.back: v = v0 + at, where v0 is initial velocity, a constant acceleration, and t elapsed time.

cards.front: What is Displacement under constant acceleration?
cards.back: Delta x = v0 t + (1/2)at^2, for constant acceleration in one dimension.

cards.front: What is Velocity-displacement relation for constant acceleration?
cards.back: v^2 = v0^2 + 2a Delta x, for constant acceleration along one axis.

cards.front: What is Displacement from average endpoint velocities?
cards.back: Delta x = [(v0 + v)/2]t, only when acceleration is constant over the interval.

cards.front: What is Horizontal projectile position?
cards.back: x = x0 + v0 cos(theta)t, neglecting air resistance and using a horizontal x-axis.

cards.front: What is Vertical projectile position?
cards.back: y = y0 + v0 sin(theta)t - (1/2)gt^2, with upward positive and constant downward gravitational acceleration g.

cards.front: What is Projectile time of flight to launch height?
cards.back: T = 2v0 sin(theta)/g, for upward launch and landing at the same height without air resistance.

cards.front: What is Projectile range on level ground?
cards.back: R = v0^2 sin(2theta)/g, with equal launch and landing heights and no air resistance.

cards.front: What is Projectile maximum height above launch point?
cards.back: H = v0^2 sin^2(theta)/(2g), for an initially upward vertical component and no air resistance.

cards.front: What is Newton's second law for constant mass?
cards.back: Net vector force = m times acceleration. Mass is constant and the reference frame is inertial.

cards.front: What is Momentum form of Newton's second law?
cards.back: Net external vector force = d(vector momentum)/dt for the system under the appropriate system definition.

cards.front: What is Weight near Earth's surface?
cards.back: Weight magnitude = mg, where g is the local gravitational acceleration; weight is a force, not mass.

cards.front: What is Maximum static friction?
cards.back: f_s,max = mu_s N. Actual static friction satisfies 0 <= f_s <= mu_s N and adjusts to prevent slipping.

cards.front: What is Kinetic friction magnitude?
cards.back: f_k = mu_k N in the elementary dry-friction model. It acts opposite relative sliding at the contact.

cards.front: What is Hooke's law for an ideal spring?
cards.back: F_x = -kx, where x is displacement from equilibrium and k the spring constant, within the spring's linear range.

cards.front: What is Force of universal gravitation?
cards.back: F = G m1 m2/r^2 for point masses or nonoverlapping spherically symmetric masses; r is center-to-center separation.

cards.front: What is Gravitational potential energy for two masses?
cards.back: U = -G M m/r, with zero potential energy at infinite separation and point or spherical masses.

cards.front: What is Change in near-surface gravitational potential energy?
cards.back: Delta U = mg Delta h, for constant g and upward height change Delta h.

cards.front: What is Work by a constant force?
cards.back: W = F d cos(theta), where theta is the angle between force and displacement.

cards.front: What is Work by a variable force along a path?
cards.back: W = integral of vector F dot d(vector r) along the path.

cards.front: What is Translational kinetic energy?
cards.back: K = (1/2)mv^2 in nonrelativistic mechanics.

cards.front: What is Work-energy theorem?
cards.back: Net work on a particle equals its change in kinetic energy: W_net = Delta K.

cards.front: What is Elastic potential energy of an ideal spring?
cards.back: U_s = (1/2)kx^2, with zero at the spring's relaxed equilibrium position.

cards.front: What is Mechanical energy conservation condition?
cards.back: K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f when only conservative forces do work on the modeled system and no other energy transfer occurs.

cards.front: What is Average power?
cards.back: P_avg = work / elapsed time, or transferred energy / elapsed time.

cards.front: What is Instantaneous mechanical power?
cards.back: P = vector F dot vector v for a force acting at the point moving with velocity v.

cards.front: What is Linear momentum?
cards.back: Vector p = m vector v for a nonrelativistic particle of mass m.

cards.front: What is Impulse?
cards.back: Vector J = integral of vector F dt = Delta vector p; for a constant force, J = F Delta t.

cards.front: What is Momentum conservation?
cards.back: Total initial momentum equals total final momentum when the net external impulse on the system is zero.

cards.front: What is Perfectly inelastic collision final velocity?
cards.back: v_f = (m1 v1 + m2 v2)/(m1 + m2) in one dimension when the objects stick and external impulse is negligible.

cards.front: What is Elastic collision conservation laws?
cards.back: Both total momentum and total kinetic energy are conserved for an isolated elastic collision.

cards.front: What is Center of mass position?
cards.back: Vector r_cm = sum of m_i vector r_i / sum of m_i, for point masses.

cards.front: What is Centripetal acceleration?
cards.back: a_c = v^2/r = omega^2 r, directed toward the center for circular motion of radius r.

cards.front: What is Net radial force for circular motion?
cards.back: F_radial = mv^2/r, directed toward the center; this is the net radial force, not an additional force type.

cards.front: What is Angular displacement and arc length?
cards.back: s = r theta, with theta in radians, for motion along a circle of radius r.

cards.front: What is Angular velocity?
cards.back: omega = dtheta/dt; its SI unit is radians per second.

cards.front: What is Tangential and angular speeds?
cards.back: v = r omega for a point rotating at distance r from a fixed axis.

cards.front: What is Tangential acceleration?
cards.back: a_t = r alpha, with angular acceleration alpha = domega/dt and fixed radius r.

cards.front: What is Torque magnitude?
cards.back: tau = rF sin(theta), where theta is the angle between the lever-arm vector and force; vector torque is r cross F.

cards.front: What is Rotational form of Newton's second law?
cards.back: Net torque about a fixed axis = I alpha, for constant moment of inertia I under the standard fixed-axis conditions.

cards.front: What is Moment of inertia of point masses?
cards.back: I = sum of m_i r_i^2, where r_i is each mass's perpendicular distance from the rotation axis.

cards.front: What is Moment of inertia of a thin hoop about its symmetry axis?
cards.back: I = MR^2, for total mass M and radius R.

cards.front: What is Moment of inertia of a uniform solid disk about its symmetry axis?
What is Moment of inertia of a uniform solid sphere about a diameter?
What is Parallel-axis theorem?
cards.back: I = I_cm + Md^2, where the new axis is parallel to the center-of-mass axis and separated by distance d.

cards.front: What is Rotational kinetic energy?
cards.back: K_rot = (1/2)I omega^2 for rotation about a fixed axis.

cards.front: What is Angular momentum of a rigid body about a fixed symmetry axis?
cards.back: L_axis = I omega; the general vector relation requires care when the angular momentum and angular velocity are not parallel.

cards.front: What is Angular momentum conservation?
cards.back: Total angular momentum stays constant when the net external torque about the chosen inertial origin is zero.

cards.front: What is Rolling without slipping condition?
cards.back: v_cm = R omega for a rigid wheel of radius R rolling on a stationary surface.

cards.front: What is Total kinetic energy of a rolling rigid body?
cards.back: K = (1/2)M v_cm^2 + (1/2)I_cm omega^2.

cards.front: What is Simple harmonic oscillator displacement?
cards.back: x(t) = A cos(omega t + phi), for ideal sinusoidal motion; A is amplitude and phi the initial phase.

cards.front: What is Acceleration in simple harmonic motion?
cards.back: a = -omega^2 x, directed toward equilibrium.

cards.front: What is Period of a mass on an ideal spring?
cards.back: T = 2pi sqrt(m/k), neglecting damping and spring mass.

cards.front: What is Period of a simple pendulum at small angles?
cards.back: T = 2pi sqrt(L/g), for a point bob, massless string, and small angular amplitude.

cards.front: What is Frequency and period?
cards.back: f = 1/T; frequency in hertz is cycles per second and period is seconds per cycle.

cards.front: What is Angular frequency and ordinary frequency?
cards.back: omega = 2pi f = 2pi/T, with omega in radians per second.

cards.front: What is Density?
cards.back: rho = mass / volume, with SI unit kg/m^3.

cards.front: What is Pressure from a perpendicular force?
cards.back: P = F_perpendicular/A; the SI unit is the pascal, equal to N/m^2.

cards.front: What is Hydrostatic pressure difference?
cards.back: P_deep - P_shallow = rho g h for an incompressible static fluid with constant density over vertical depth h.

cards.front: What is Buoyant force?
cards.back: F_b = rho_fluid g V_displaced, equal to the weight of displaced fluid, under hydrostatic conditions.

cards.front: What is Continuity for incompressible steady flow?
cards.back: A1 v1 = A2 v2 along a flow tube, using mean flow speeds and no leakage.

cards.front: What is Volume flow rate?
cards.back: Q = A v_avg for flow through cross-sectional area A with mean perpendicular speed v_avg.

cards.front: What is Bernoulli's equation?
cards.back: P + (1/2)rho v^2 + rho gy = constant along a streamline in steady, incompressible, inviscid flow with no added or removed mechanical energy.

cards.front: What is Poiseuille flow through a circular tube?
cards.back: Q = pi r^4 Delta P/(8 eta L), for steady laminar flow of a Newtonian fluid in a long rigid tube of radius r and length L.

cards.front: What is Stokes drag on a sphere?
cards.back: F_drag = 6pi eta r v for a sphere of radius r moving slowly through a viscous fluid at very low Reynolds number, far from boundaries.

cards.front: What is Heat for a temperature change without a phase change?
cards.back: Q = mc Delta T, with approximately constant specific heat c over the temperature interval.

cards.front: What is Latent heat during a phase change?
cards.back: Q = mL, where L is the relevant specific latent heat and the phase change occurs under the specified conditions.

cards.front: What is Linear thermal expansion?
cards.back: Delta L = alpha L0 Delta T for small temperature changes with approximately constant linear expansion coefficient alpha.

cards.front: What is Ideal gas law?
cards.back: PV = nRT = N k_B T, with absolute temperature T, n moles, and N particles.

cards.front: What is First law of thermodynamics with work done by the system?
cards.back: Delta U = Q - W, where Q is heat entering the system and W is work done by the system on its surroundings.

cards.front: What is Quasistatic pressure-volume work?
cards.back: W_by = integral P dV for work done by the system against the matching external pressure in a quasistatic process; expansion gives positive work.

cards.front: What is Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas?
cards.back: U = (3/2)nRT, ignoring electronic excitation and choosing the conventional thermal-energy reference.

cards.front: What is Isothermal work by an ideal gas in reversible expansion?
cards.back: W_by = nRT ln(V_f/V_i), with constant absolute temperature T.

cards.front: What is Reversible adiabatic relation for an ideal gas?
cards.back: PV^gamma = constant, for constant heat capacities and gamma = C_P/C_V.

cards.front: What is Molar heat-capacity difference for an ideal gas?
cards.back: C_P - C_V = R, where the heat capacities are per mole.

cards.front: What is Heat engine efficiency?
cards.back: eta = W_net,out/Q_hot = 1 - Q_cold,out/Q_hot, with heat magnitudes taken positive over a full cycle.

cards.front: What is Carnot efficiency?
cards.back: eta_C = 1 - T_cold/T_hot, using absolute temperatures, for a reversible engine between two reservoirs.

cards.front: What is Refrigerator coefficient of performance?
cards.back: COP_R = Q_cold,in/W_in, the heat removed from the cold region divided by work input per cycle.

cards.front: What is Heat pump coefficient of performance?
cards.back: COP_HP = Q_hot,out/W_in, the heat delivered to the warm region divided by work input per cycle.

cards.front: What is Entropy change along a reversible path?
cards.back: Delta S = integral dQ_rev/T, with T the absolute temperature at which reversible heat transfer occurs.

cards.front: What is Entropy change for reversible isothermal heat transfer?
cards.back: Delta S = Q_rev/T, at constant absolute temperature T.

cards.front: What is Thermal conduction through a plane slab?
cards.back: Heat-transfer rate = k A Delta T/L for steady one-dimensional conduction, with thermal conductivity k and thickness L.

cards.front: What is Stefan-Boltzmann net thermal radiation?
cards.back: P_net = epsilon sigma A(T^4 - T_surroundings^4) for a gray surface exchanging radiation with large uniform surroundings under the model's assumptions.

cards.front: What is Wien's displacement law?
cards.back: lambda_max T = b for the wavelength form of a blackbody spectrum; b is approximately 2.898 x 10^-3 m K.

cards.front: What is Root-mean-square speed of ideal gas molecules?
cards.back: v_rms = sqrt(3k_B T/m) = sqrt(3RT/M), with single-particle mass m or molar mass M in kg/mol.

cards.front: What is Wave speed, frequency, and wavelength?
cards.back: v = f lambda for a periodic wave; v is phase speed, f frequency, and lambda wavelength.

cards.front: What is Wave speed on a stretched string?
cards.back: v = sqrt(Tension/mu), with linear mass density mu and small transverse disturbances on an ideal string.

cards.front: What is Intensity of an isotropic point source?
cards.back: I = P/(4pi r^2), assuming power P spreads uniformly without absorption.

cards.front: What is Sound intensity level?
cards.back: beta = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels, commonly using I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 in air.

cards.front: What is Beat frequency?
cards.back: f_beat = absolute value of f1 - f2 for two nearby frequencies.

cards.front: What is Standing-wave frequencies on a string fixed at both ends?
cards.back: f_n = n v/(2L), for n = 1, 2, 3, and so on, with string length L.

cards.front: What is Standing-wave frequencies in an ideal open-open air column?
cards.back: f_n = n v/(2L), for n = 1, 2, 3, and so on, neglecting end corrections.

cards.front: What is Standing-wave frequencies in an ideal closed-open air column?
cards.back: f_n = n v/(4L), for odd n = 1, 3, 5, and so on, neglecting end corrections.

cards.front: What is Doppler shift for sound with source and observer approaching?
cards.back: f_observed = f_source(v + v_observer)/(v - v_source), using approach speeds relative to the medium and subsonic source motion along the line of sight.

cards.front: What is Index of refraction?
cards.back: n = c/v, with vacuum light speed c and phase speed v in the medium at the specified frequency.

cards.front: What is Snell's law?
cards.back: n1 sin(theta1) = n2 sin(theta2), with angles measured from the normal to the interface.

cards.front: What is Critical angle for total internal reflection?
cards.back: theta_c = arcsin(n2/n1), for light incident from index n1 into lower index n2; total internal reflection occurs above theta_c.

cards.front: What is Thin-lens equation?
cards.back: 1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i in paraxial optics. With the real-is-positive convention, real objects and real images have positive distances and converging lenses have positive f.

cards.front: What is Thin-lens transverse magnification?
cards.back: m = h_i/h_o = -d_i/d_o, using a consistent real-is-positive distance convention; negative m means an inverted image.

cards.front: What is Optical power of a lens?
cards.back: P_optical = 1/f with focal length in meters, giving power in diopters; the sign follows that of f.

cards.front: What is Double-slit bright-fringe condition?
cards.back: d sin(theta) = m lambda for two coherent in-phase narrow slits, integer m, and far-field observation.

cards.front: What is Double-slit fringe spacing at small angles?
cards.back: Delta y = lambda L/d, for screen distance L much larger than slit separation d and small observation angles.

cards.front: What is Single-slit diffraction minima?
cards.back: a sin(theta) = m lambda, for nonzero integers m, slit width a, and far-field diffraction.

cards.front: What is Diffraction grating principal maxima?
cards.back: d sin(theta) = m lambda for normal incidence, slit spacing d, and integer order m within the allowed angular range.

cards.front: What is Malus's law?
cards.back: I = I0 cos^2(theta), for linearly polarized light passing through an ideal analyzer at angle theta to the polarization direction.

cards.front: What is Coulomb force magnitude?
cards.back: F = k_e absolute value of q1 q2 / r^2, for point charges in vacuum; like charges repel and unlike charges attract.

cards.front: What is Electric field definition?
cards.back: Vector E = vector F/q_test for a positive test charge small enough not to disturb the source configuration.

cards.front: What is Electric field magnitude of a point charge?
cards.back: E = k_e absolute value of Q/r^2 in vacuum; the direction is outward for positive Q and inward for negative Q.

cards.front: What is Electric potential of a point charge?
cards.back: V = k_e Q/r with zero potential at infinity, for a point charge in vacuum.

cards.front: What is Electric potential energy of two point charges?
cards.back: U = k_e q1 q2/r, with zero at infinite separation; charge signs are retained.

cards.front: What is Electric potential difference and field?
cards.back: V_b - V_a = -integral from a to b of vector E dot d(vector l), for an electrostatic field.

cards.front: What is Gauss's law for electricity?
cards.back: Closed-surface integral of vector E dot d(vector A) = Q_enclosed/epsilon0, in vacuum using total enclosed charge.

cards.front: What is Capacitance?
cards.back: C = Q/V, where Q is the magnitude of charge on either conductor and V is the potential difference for an ideal linear capacitor.

cards.front: What is Parallel-plate capacitance?
cards.back: C = epsilon A/d, neglecting edge effects, with uniform dielectric permittivity epsilon and plate separation d.

cards.front: What is Energy stored in a capacitor?
cards.back: U = (1/2)CV^2 = Q^2/(2C) = (1/2)QV for a linear capacitor.

cards.front: What is Capacitors in parallel?
cards.back: C_eq = sum of C_i, because each capacitor has the same voltage.

cards.front: What is Capacitors in series?
cards.back: 1/C_eq = sum of 1/C_i for ideal series capacitors carrying equal charge magnitude.

cards.front: What is Electric current?
cards.back: I = dQ/dt, the rate of charge flow through a cross section.

cards.front: What is Ohm's law for an ohmic component?
cards.back: V = IR when resistance R remains constant under the stated conditions.

cards.front: What is Resistance of a uniform wire?
cards.back: R = rho_e L/A, with resistivity rho_e, length L, and cross-sectional area A.

cards.front: What is Resistors in series?
cards.back: R_eq = sum of R_i, since the same current passes through each resistor.

cards.front: What is Resistors in parallel?
cards.back: 1/R_eq = sum of 1/R_i, since each resistor has the same potential difference.

cards.front: What is Electric power in a resistor?
cards.back: P = IV = I^2 R = V^2/R for an ohmic resistor, taking dissipated power as positive.

cards.front: What is Kirchhoff's junction rule?
cards.back: The algebraic sum of currents at a junction is zero; total current entering equals total current leaving in the lumped steady-circuit model.

cards.front: What is Kirchhoff's loop rule?
cards.back: The algebraic sum of potential changes around a closed circuit loop is zero when any induced emf is properly included in the circuit model.

cards.front: What is RC time constant?
cards.back: tau = RC, with resistance R and capacitance C in an ideal first-order RC circuit.

cards.front: What is Discharging capacitor voltage?
cards.back: V(t) = V0 e^(-t/RC), for an initially charged capacitor discharging through a resistor with no source.

cards.front: What is Charging capacitor voltage from zero?
cards.back: V_C(t) = V_source[1 - e^(-t/RC)] for a DC step applied to an initially uncharged series RC circuit.

cards.front: What is Magnetic force on a moving point charge?
cards.back: Vector F_B = q(vector v cross vector B); magnitude is absolute value of q times vB sin(theta).

cards.front: What is Magnetic force on a straight current segment?
cards.back: Vector F = I(vector L cross vector B) in a uniform magnetic field; vector L points with conventional current.

cards.front: What is Magnetic field of a long straight wire?
cards.back: B = mu0 I/(2pi r) in vacuum outside an ideal long straight wire, at perpendicular distance r.

cards.front: What is Magnetic field inside an ideal long solenoid?
cards.back: B = mu0 n I in vacuum, with n turns per unit length, far from the ends.

cards.front: What is Magnetic flux through a flat area?
cards.back: Phi_B = BA cos(theta) for uniform B, where theta is the angle between B and the area's normal.

cards.front: What is Faraday's law for an N-turn coil?
cards.back: Emf = -N dPhi_B/dt when each turn links the same flux; the minus sign expresses Lenz's law.

cards.front: What is Energy stored in an ideal inductor?
cards.back: U = (1/2)LI^2, with inductance L and current I.

cards.front: What is Speed of light in vacuum?
cards.back: c = 299,792,458 m/s exactly in SI.

cards.front: What is Elementary charge magnitude?
cards.back: e = 1.602176634 x 10^-19 C exactly in SI. An electron has charge -e.

cards.front: What is Planck constant?
cards.back: h = 6.62607015 x 10^-34 J s exactly in SI; the reduced Planck constant is h/(2pi).

cards.front: What is Boltzmann constant?
cards.back: k_B = 1.380649 x 10^-23 J/K exactly in SI.

cards.front: What is Avogadro constant?
cards.back: N_A = 6.02214076 x 10^23 mol^-1 exactly in SI.

cards.front: What is Universal gravitational constant?
cards.back: G is approximately 6.67430 x 10^-11 m^3 kg^-1 s^-2; it is experimentally measured, not an exact defining constant.

cards.front: What is Molar gas constant?
cards.back: R = N_A k_B = 8.31446261815324 J mol^-1 K^-1 exactly from the SI defining constants.

cards.front: What is Photon energy?
cards.back: E = hf = hc/lambda in vacuum, where h is Planck's constant and lambda is vacuum wavelength.

cards.front: What is De Broglie wavelength?
cards.back: lambda = h/p, with p the particle's momentum magnitude; use relativistic momentum when necessary.

cards.front: What is Photoelectric maximum kinetic energy?
cards.back: K_max = hf - work function for emitted electrons when hf is at least the work function, in the elementary single-photon model.

cards.front: What is Mass-energy equivalence at rest?
cards.back: E0 = mc^2, where m is rest mass and E0 rest energy.

cards.front: What is Radioactive decay law?
cards.back: N(t) = N0 e^(-lambda_d t), with constant decay constant lambda_d and no production of the nuclide.

cards.front: What is Half-life and decay constant?
cards.back: t_half = ln(2)/lambda_d for exponential radioactive decay.

cards.front: What is Radioactive activity?
cards.back: A = lambda_d N = -dN/dt, with SI unit becquerel, equal to one decay per second.

cards.front: What is Lorentz factor?
cards.back: gamma = 1/sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2), for relative inertial speed v less than c.
